routes.name: The Prow (Kit Carson)
routes.overview: A knob-style classic on Kit Carson's south ridge. The hardest move comes at once, over a serious roof at the foot; the next two leads (5.6) sidestep a bulge, staying right of the crest, and everything above is mellower.

routes.name: The Prow (Kit Carson)
routes.fa: ?Paul Spanjer & Jody Schoberlein, July, 1980? [Alan Haverfeld and Dave Mazel, early 1980s]
routes.overview: A top-notch knob outing in the Crestones where commitment arrives suddenly once on the arete. The many upper leads run about 5.3 to 5.4 and the edge keeps rising, making completion the best way out. Once on the little summit of the Prow, head northward onto the ledge system that continues toward the true summit.
routes.crux: gymnastic move over the overhang at the very start (5.8)
variations: Skip the bottom overhang by climbing easier slabs a couple of hundred yards over to the right, joining the edge higher up

routes.name: East Face Variation
routes.fa: M. Preiss and D. Preiss, Winter 1995
routes.season: Dec-Apr (winter-spring; condition-dependent), first climbed in winter
gear: medium alpine rock rack to 3in (doubles in small cams)
hazards: Avalanche hazard on the Source Lake basin approach below the East Face — check the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast first
PG13 grade denotes sustained runout climbing with real injury potential on a fall
Rockfall potential from above on the East Face
Steep unconsolidated snow on the final pitch can be avalanche- or slough-prone
routes.overview: A 5-pitch, PG13 winter mixed/ice line that follows the summer East Face for its first two pitches before breaking left onto steeper, more sustained rock/ice ground and a runout crux pitch to reach the top.
routes.beta: Begins on the line of the summer East Face for roughly two pitches, then traverses left about 30 ft with limited protection into a corner below a steep rock barrier. The crux pitch climbs this corner at about 5.8-ish with one short aid move (A0) or M5 mixed climbing to a tree belay, after which a final pitch of steep snow (using small trees for anchors) trends slightly right to finish near the summit. accounts describe the line in these general sections rather than a strict pitch-by-pitch account across all 5 rope-lengths. Rated Grade III, PG13, reflecting sustained runout climbing on marginal protection.
routes.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time given the runout, condition-dependent crux pitch and the need to complete the South Face rappel descent and basin exit before dark; back off early if ice/snow coverage on the crux corner looks thin or the approach shows avalanche warning signs.
routes.rappels: Descend via the South Face rappel route (shared anchors/gear with the South Face descent; 60m rope recommended)
routes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.

waypoints.name: Alpental Parking Lot
waypoints.note: Park at Alpental ski area (I-90 Exit 52); take the Source Lake trail, then head into the basin below The Tooth's east face.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 Exit 52 and follow Alpental Road about a mile and a half north to its end at the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead, parking in the Alpental ski area lot at roughly 3,100 ft. The Source Lake trail leaves from the lot, and in winter you are hiking or skinning from the car. Read the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast before you drive up — the basin you approach through is avalanche terrain and that read is a pre-trip requirement, not an option.

waypoints.name: The Tooth
waypoints.note: Steeper winter variation on the east face (AI3-4/M4-5) reaching the same summit as the standard South Face route.

routes.detailed_rack: A medium winter alpine rock rack to 3 inches with doubles in the small cam sizes, extra runners/slings, a helmet, and two ice tools for the mixed and ice sections; 60m rope for the South Face rappel descent.
what_to_bring: approach skis or snowshoes for the Source Lake basin approach
map/GPS for basin navigation in poor visibility
pro_tips: Treat the traverse into the crux corner as unprotected and climb it accordingly
A stretch of cold, settled weather after a snow-loading storm typically gives the best mixed/ice coverage
Carry a 60m rope to use the South Face's fixed chain rap anchors at Pineapple Pass on descent
Because this is a winter-conditions-dependent variation, check recent trip reports before committing
routes.watch_out:
Significant avalanche danger on approach; avoid summer trail during winter (high hazard zone); use east face approach to Source Lake
Steep slab climbing with mixed grade M4-5 sections; requires solid mixed climbing ability on exposed terrain
Second pitch features long run-outs on thin ice with difficult screw/picket protection; high consequence if placements fail
Balancy mixed terrain over exposed east face; slipping on slab sections over significant drops
Rime ice buildup on exposed pitches; weather deterioration common in Snoqualmie Pass area
Corniced terrain on descent; rappel hazards with potential rime/ice accumulation on anchor points
routes.pro_needs: Protection is limited on the ~30 ft traverse into the crux corner and thin through the mixed crux itself; carry doubles in small cams plus extra slings to extend runners over featured but sparsely protectable rock.
routes.best_season: Winter-spring (roughly December-April) once enough snow and ice have built up on the upper pitches to protect and climb the mixed ground; as a route first climbed in winter conditions (1995), it is inherently condition-dependent and not consistently in on a given date.
routes.aid_grade: A0 (one short aid move noted on the crux pitch)
routes.approach: From the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead (~3,100 ft, 1.5 mi north of I-90 Exit 52 via Alpental Rd), hike/skin up the main trail toward Source Lake, then turn south into the valley/basin below The Tooth's east face. In winter, avoid the summer approach path/gully directly below the East Face due to significant avalanche danger; approach via the broader basin instead.
routes.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the South Face line, using its tree/gear anchors and the two bolted chain rappel stations at Pineapple Pass lower down (60m rope recommended), then hike/ski back out through the basin to Source Lake and the Alpental trailhead.
routes.bail: Rappel the line of ascent using gear or tree anchors from any belay; retreat is most straightforward before committing to the crux corner pitch, since the runout traverse into it is hard to protect on the way back.

pitch_detail.notes: Follows the standard summer East Face route for roughly the first two pitches before breaking off it.
Traverses left ~30 ft with limited protection into a corner, then climbs the crux corner to a tree belay.
Finishes on steep snow using small trees for anchors, trending slightly right to top out near the summit.

routes.itinerary: A single long winter/spring day: early approach from Alpental through the Source Lake basin to the base of the East Face, 5 pitches of mixed/ice/snow climbing, then rappelling the South Face and returning via the same basin approach.

access.fees: $5 day-use fee or valid Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Pass at the Alpental/Snow Lake trailhead. In winter the Alpental lot runs under the privately-operated 'Park at the Summit' program, which charges roughly $25/vehicle only on weekends and a handful of holidays (late Nov into spring) rather than a flat daily rate — the NW Forest Pass is not accepted on those specific paid days. Carpools of 3+ can often park free as space allows.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required for day/overnight use May 15-Oct 31; not required for winter ascents outside that window
access.closures: No seasonal road closure (Alpental Rd/I-90 plowed year-round); temporary avalanche-related backcountry closures possible after major storms
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District — Alpine Lakes Wilderness

road.driveNote: Roughly 45 min-1 hour from Seattle via I-90 to Exit 52.
road.seasonalGate: Winter/spring routes are climbed precisely because of seasonal snow; the access road itself is generally kept open for the ski area, though avalanche hazard affects the approach trail.

climate.spring: Consolidating snowpack can offer workable mixed/snow conditions March-May, but the crux corner's ice/snow coverage is highly variable
climate.summer: Route reverts to being climbed as a summer East Face rock variation rather than this winter mixed line
climate.winter: Primary season (Dec-Mar) for the route as a mixed/ice line, with the highest avalanche danger on approach after new snow or wind loading
climate.typical: Wet, maritime Cascade climate; heavy wet winter snowfall drives frequent avalanche hazard on the approach

emergency.notes: King County Sheriff's Search and Rescue (volunteer, no charge) coordinates alpine rescues in the Alpental/Snoqualmie Pass area; cell coverage in the Alpental valley/ski area is generally usable but can be unreliable higher on the peak.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead (~3,100 ft), at the end of Alpental Road off I-90 Exit 52

rappel_detail.notes: First rappel down the upper South Face on a natural tree or gear anchor, joining the shared South Face descent line used by several routes on this side of the peak.
Continues down the face on natural anchors toward easier ground above Pineapple Pass.
First of two bolted chain rap stations near Pineapple Pass; a 60m rope is recommended through this section.
Second chain station, dropping to the basin/talus below Pineapple Pass; from there hike or ski out toward Source Lake and the Alpental trailhead.

routes.rappel_count_note: Descends via The Tooth's shared South Face rap line; reported as ~4 rappels combining upper tree/gear anchors with two bolted chain stations lower down near Pineapple Pass (one party describes 4 raps on one rope, or 2 on twin ropes, with sling anchors on trees/boulders). Individual per-station lengths beyond the ~4-rap, single-60m-rope total aren't known, so no per-station length is shown.

approach_variants.name: Alpental into the basin below the east face, avoiding the summer gully in winter
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental / Snow Lake trailhead at about 3,100 ft, hike or skin toward Source Lake, then turn south into the basin beneath The Tooth's east face. In winter, do not use the summer approach path and gully that run directly below the east face. That line is avalanche terrain and the NWAC Snoqualmie Pass forecast is the pre-trip read, not an optional one. Take the broader basin instead and come at the face from open ground. About 3.2 km and 2,500 ft to the top.
approach_variants.season: Roughly December to April, and only when the upper mixed ground has built up enough snow and ice to climb and protect — first climbed in winter 1995 and genuinely condition-dependent
hazards: Avalanche danger in the Source Lake basin and specifically in the summer gully below the east face — take the broad basin in winter
PG13: sustained runout climbing on marginal protection with real injury potential
Rockfall from above onto the east face
Steep unconsolidated snow on the final pitch, prone to sloughing
The descent is the South Face rappel line, shared with other parties, on a short winter day
approach_variants.baseFinding: This route starts on the summer East Face, so finding the East Face is the whole problem, and the answer is to go past the South Face start. From the notch at the top of Pineapple Pass, where the South Face begins, walk right (north) along the base, underneath the east face. That is the published direction and it is a walk, not a climb. What the first two pitches should feel like: fourth class to about 5.5, on sub-par rock with tricky protection. Easy ground that is hard to protect is right for this face. If pitch one is clean and well protected you are somewhere else on the mountain. The move that separates this from the summer route, and the point at which you will know for certain: after roughly two pitches on the summer line, this variation traverses left about 30 ft, with little protection on the traverse, into a corner sitting below a steep rock barrier. That corner is the crux — 5.8-ish with one aid move, or M5 when it is iced. A leftward traverse into a corner under a barrier means you are on the variation; carrying straight on up means you are on the summer East Face. And the finish confirms it: the last pitch is steep snow, belayed off small trees, trending slightly right to finish near the summit. A rock finish is the summer route. Honest limit: accounts describe this line in these blocks rather than pitch by pitch. If the ice is not there, there is no route to find, and that is a real answer rather than a route-finding failure.

routes.name: Klawatti Peak SW Buttress
routes.fa: Lloyd Anderson, Karl Boyer, Tom Gorton — July 7, 1940 (also the peak's first ascent)
hazards: Loose rock on the buttress — test holds carefully
Crevasses on the glacier approach to Klawatti Col
routes.overview: A moderate alpine rock line up Klawatti Peak's southwest buttress from Klawatti Col — 2-3 short low-5th-class pitches leading to scrambling on the summit.
routes.beta: From Klawatti Col, climb the SW Buttress via 2-3 short low-5th-class pitches with easier scrambling above to the summit; rock quality requires testing holds carefully.
routes.turnaround: Given the loose rock, turn back or slow down if holds feel questionable rather than pushing through — this is a route where rockfall/handhold failure, not time pressure, is the main hazard driver.
routes.rappels: Downclimb or rappel the route on gear anchors/slings; alternate descent via the Smokestack gully to a rappel station accessing the McAllister Glacier
routes.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
routes.comms: Cell service is unreliable to absent in the Inspiration/Klawatti Glacier basin; carry a satellite communicator or PLB.
routes.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
waypoints.directions: From Seattle, take I-5 north then follow WA-20, the North Cascades Highway, east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20 — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way. Any overnight stay in the Eldorado/Klawatti zone requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available in advance on Recreation.gov or as a limited walk-up allocation from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or ranger station.

waypoints.name: Eldorado (East Ridge) camp
waypoints.directions: Cross the Cascade River near the trailhead on whatever log or ford is in that year, then climb the steep, unmaintained climbers' path through old growth to the boulder field and on into the Eldorado Creek and Roush Creek basin. Rope up there and climb the Eldorado Glacier to camp on the ice cap near the base of Eldorado's east ridge.

waypoints.name: Klawatti camp / col
waypoints.note: Camp south of Klawatti near the col dividing the Klawatti and McAllister Glaciers; SW Buttress start is minutes away.
waypoints.directions: Roped, traverse the Inspiration Glacier north-northeast past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti Col, the saddle between the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on the peak's south side. The ice cap is flat and featureless and whiteouts are common, so carry a bearing or track.

waypoints.name: Klawatti Peak
waypoints.directions: The buttress stands minutes above the col camp. Cross the moat onto the rock, climb one to three short low-fifth pitches of loose rock up the buttress, then scramble along the elongated southwest crest to the summit, where the high point is not obvious.

timing.recommendedStart: Climbed as a summit-day outing directly from the Klawatti/icecap camp, typically alongside a broader Eldorado-Klawatti icecap traverse

routes.detailed_rack: A single light rack to 2 inches with several slings for anchors covers the 2-3 short pitches.
pro_tips: Camp near Klawatti Col to combine this with Austera Peak and/or Eldorado's other routes in one trip
watch_out: Rock quality is inconsistent; treat holds with suspicion
routes.pro_needs: Light rack to 2 inches; test holds carefully due to loose rock on the buttress.
routes.best_season: Standard North Cascades icecap season; best once the Inspiration/Klawatti Glacier approach and Klawatti Col are safely crossable, typically July through September.
routes.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From camp, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) climbing the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap, typically another 3-5 hours. Any overnight stay requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Important — this route is not on Eldorado Peak itself: from the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600ft), continue traversing the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit to Klawatti col; Tepeh Towers are passed along this same glacier traverse, and Austera Peak requires further travel across the Klawatti Glacier (including a short rappel from the col) beyond Klawatti Peak — meaningfully further and more committing than simply topping out on Eldorado.
routes.descent_text: Either reverse the ascent line, or descend north through a gully toward a rock feature known as The Smokestack, circle it clockwise to grassy ledges, descend the north ridge to the Klawatti Glacier, and follow glacier travel to the McAllister Glacier rappel station.
routes.bail: The route is short (3 pitches); retreat by downclimbing or rappelling the line climbed is straightforward at any point.

pitch_detail.notes: The route starts on the southwest side of the peak, minutes from the camp spots south of Klawatti. The first problem is the moat: it widens every summer as the glacier shrinks, so scout for a snow bridge or a step across onto rock. The first pitch climbs short low-fifth-class rock straight off the moat. The rock is loose in places, so test holds before weighting them.

One or two more short low-fifth pitches continue up the buttress. How much roped climbing there is depends on the moat and the line chosen: at least one account finds only the bottom pitch fifth class, with steep, loose class 4 above. Belays are built from gear and slings, with a single rack to 2 inches.

Once on the southwest ridge the angle eases to a scramble along an elongated summit crest, where the high point is not obvious. Keep testing holds. For the descent, downclimb or rappel the route, backing up any old anchors with fresh slings, or go down the north side past The Smokestack to the Klawatti Glacier.

routes.itinerary: Typically climbed as a quick add-on from an established Klawatti/icecap camp (see the Southeast Face route's 3-day traverse itinerary): approach and camp on Day 1-2, then climb the SW Buttress in 1-2 hours on a summit day alongside or instead of the south face.

access.fees: $10 per person recreation fee for backcountry camping (free for ages 15 and under); a separate non-refundable $6 fee applies only if booking through the online reservation/lottery system.
access.rules: Bear-resistant food storage required; Leave No Trace camping (no fires above treeline on the glacier approach); stay on the established climbers' trail on the lower approach to limit erosion.
access.permit: wilderness/camping permit required for any overnight stay off-road; obtain in person (walk-up, first-come) or online in advance via recreation.gov. Klawatti sits in a cross-country zone, not one of the park's quota-lottery zones (e.g., Sahale, Copper Ridge), so walk-up permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center are normally available.
access.closures: Cascade River Road beyond the trailhead is gated/unplowed in winter and frequently has blowdowns or washouts in spring before it's cleared — check current road status before driving.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park / Stephen Mather Wilderness (National Park Service)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or none required for Cascade River Road trailhead parking (day use)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount; $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee.

road.name: Cascade River Road (from Marblemount) to Boston Basin/Eldorado trailhead area
road.status: Paved for the first ~10 miles from Marblemount, then gravel with potholes and washboard; passenger cars can often reach mile ~18 (NP boundary) but a high-clearance vehicle is recommended for the final miles to the Eldorado TH/Boston Basin pulloff (~mile 20-21.7). Vulnerable to washouts/flooding closures, especially in spring and after heavy rain.

road.seasonalGate: Only snow-cleared and opened each spring/early summer; check the NPS North Cascades road-conditions page before driving.

climate.summer: Main season; approach largely snow-free by August
climate.forecastZone: NWS Zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes)

emergency.notes: Cell coverage unreliable in this basin; rescue may take hours to days
emergency.rangerStation: Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount, WA
emergency.nearestHospital: Skagit Valley Hospital, 300 Hospital Pkwy, Mount Vernon, WA, (360) 424-4111
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Skagit County Sheriff's Office (360) 336-9450; NCNP dispatch (360) 856-5700 ext. 515 business hours / (360) 873-4590 ext. 37 after hours

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through August, when the sunny buttress is dry and Klawatti Col is still a snow walk away

July.reason: The south-west-facing rock dries early in the month while the Inspiration Glacier still has good bridges up to Klawatti Col.

June.reason: The glacier approach is filled in, but the buttress ledges still hold snow and the col and summit are often corniced.

August.reason: The buttress is dry and warm; crevasses on the approach open wider late in the month, so routefinding takes longer.

October.reason: Snow on the ledges and bare ice on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers make both the climb and approach hazardous.

September.reason: Rock stays dry, but the glacier approach becomes icy with open crevasses and the days shorten on a long icecap trip.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Eldorado Creek trailhead lot at mile 20 on Cascade River Road (~2,100 ft)

approach_variants.name: Eldorado ice cap to Klawatti Col, then the buttress that stands directly above camp
approach_variants.notes: The whole approach is the Eldorado one: Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead near 2,100 ft, the river crossing, the steep unmaintained boot path through old growth to the boulder field, and up into Eldorado Creek / Roush Creek basin. Camp there or push on to the Eldorado-Inspiration Glacier camp near 7,500-7,600 ft. From that camp the day is glacier travel, not a trail. Rope up, cross the Inspiration Glacier well past Eldorado's summit, and continue north-northeast to Klawatti Col at about 7,800 ft, the saddle dividing the Klawatti and McAllister glaciers on Klawatti Peak's south side. This traverse is the navigational crux of the whole route — it is flat, featureless and whiteouts are routine, so carry a bearing or a track and be prepared to navigate blind. Parties commonly camp at the col itself. Three Klawatti routes leave from cols within half a mile of each other. A wilderness permit for the Klawatti zone comes from the Marblemount ranger station.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the Inspiration Glacier traverse and the moat at the foot of the buttress are reliably crossable
hazards: Crevasses on the Eldorado and Inspiration glaciers, worst near Eldorado's east ridge
Whiteout navigation on a flat, featureless ice cap with no handrail
A moat at the foot of the buttress where the glacier has pulled back from the rock
Rock repeatedly described as lousy and loose — test every hold rather than trusting the grade
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The buttress stands directly above the Klawatti camp and is minutes from it — not a traverse away. That is the first thing that separates it from the peak's other two routes. If you have walked more than a few minutes from the saddle you have started the wrong climb.

The deciding test is what is above the moat, and it is a one-look test. Cross the moat and the ground above is rock and keeps being rock: two or three short low-fifth pitches, then class 4, then scrambling. If there are several hundred feet of 40-55 degree snow above a short rock step, you are on the south-facing snow line known as the southeast face, which starts from the same col and is a snow climb with one rock move rather than a rock climb. That difference decides whether you needed a rack or a second tool.

The third route is at a different col entirely. The North Ridge starts from the Klawatti-Austera col at about 7,900 ft, roughly 0.4 mile further along under Klawatti's west face — a separate notch a hundred feet higher, and one you have to solve rather than walk through. If you are walking a ridge crest north with a rock tower ahead of you, you have gone past this route to that one.

What the col looks like: a broad saddle with usable bivy sites on the south side, and the low point between the Klawatti Glacier on one side and the McAllister on the other — so from it you can see down both. A spot where the ground only falls away one way is not the col.

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a different cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

routes.name: Northeast Slabs
gear: Cams (to at least ~2 in) for rock protection where available
Skis or snowshoes for the approach (optional)
hazards: Crux Pitch 2 is an essentially unprotectable ~30m horizontal traverse on 50-60° snow/ice — serious fall consequences if it goes
Avalanche terrain on the Source Lake approach and the snow cone below the route
Conditions swing widely year to year — can range from solid neve to bare rock and verglas
Possible cornices near the summit ridge in heavy-snow years
Short winter daylight hours
routes.overview: This is the peak's documented winter/spring mixed line on the northeast side, generally referred to as the Northeast Slab (the name 'Catscratch Couloir' is not established for The Tooth, and does not appear in any coverage of this peak). It's a roughly 5-6 pitch snow/neve/ice/rock route close to the Alpental trailhead, giving a quick winter alpine outing when conditions are in — but the character swings widely year to year from good neve to bare rock and verglas.
routes.beta: No route on The Tooth is actually named 'Catscratch Couloir.' The physical description (NE-facing, winter ice/mixed line) matches the well-documented 'Northeast Slabs' route exactly, so the beta below describes Northeast Slabs. It climbs the NE-side slabs (originally graded around WI3, 50-70° ice on the first pitch, though conditions vary year to year), with a difficult-to-protect second pitch of thin ice and balancey mixed slab climbing, onto the North Ridge, finishing with a low-5th-class/M3 pitch over a notch on the east face before easier ground to the summit.
routes.turnaround: Given avalanche exposure on the approach and sparse, difficult protection on the crux pitch, set a conservative turnaround time and be willing to bail if ice conditions are thin, the avalanche forecast is elevated, or the party is moving slower than planned.
routes.rock_grade: Low 5th class (5th-class rock sections; M3 notch traverse)
routes.rappels: Standard descent follows the South Face rappel line (4 raps, roughly 25-30m each) back to Pineapple Pass; some winter parties instead make 2 long rappels (60m) from a tree below the summit directly down to the notch before skiing out.
routes.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
routes.descent: Descend the standard South Face rappels
obj_haz: Unprotectable slab traverse on thin ice/snow
Highly condition-dependent (route can be out of shape)
Exposed low-5th/M3 rock step through the summit notch

waypoints.name: Alpental / Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: I-90 Exit 52, Alpental ski area parking lot; approach up valley past Source Lake toward Pineapple Pass basin for NE Face/Catscratch Couloir.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 and head north on Alpental Road to the Alpental Ski Area, where the trailhead starts from the parking lot at about 3,100 feet.

waypoints.name: Northeast Slabs base
waypoints.directions: Follow the Snow Lake Trail up the valley toward Source Lake. Once there is real snow cover, keep to the valley bottom rather than the summer switchbacks, which cross avalanche paths. Past Source Lake, traverse the talus below the cliff band toward the Tooth's northeast side, then climb the snow finger into the basin beneath the face and up the snow slope to the foot of the gully where the route starts; cache skis at the bottom of that slope. Roughly 2 to 2.5 miles and 1,500 to 2,000 ft from the car.

waypoints.name: The Tooth summit
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully and the slabs above it, five to six pitches of snow, ice and low fifth-class rock, to the North Ridge, then make the exposed move over the notch on the east face and follow easier ground to the summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: Approach via the Source Lake trail (often skinned or skied in winter), then traverse south into the valley below The Tooth's east face to the base of the Northeast Slabs. Climb 5-6…

routes.detailed_rack: Screws, pickets, and a small rock rack for mixed steps and belays
pro_tips: Manage avalanche hazard on the Source Lake approach
Bring gear to rappel the standard South Face on descent
routes.watch_out:
Significant avalanche danger on approach to The Tooth; avoid summer path entirely due to high avalanche exposure
Second pitch protection difficulties; long run-outs on thin ice with inadequate screw/picket placement options; high consequences for protection failure
Balancy mixed slab climbing requiring precise footwork; exposed low 5th class/M3 pitch over east face; 50-70 degree ice sections
Early season ascents face steeper avalanche risk on approach gully; spring warming creates slough and slab hazards
Rime ice accumulation on exposed upper pitches reduces friction and increases slipping risk; direct north aspect can produce rime ice in winter storms
Weather exposure on approach valley; compressed daylight window for winter climbs increases risk of descent in darkness
routes.pro_needs: Ice and rock pro for the mixed terrain
routes.best_season: Winter through early spring in a stable, well-bonded snow year — documented ascents have gone in February. The line only 'goes' safely when there's enough snow/ice adhesion on the unprotected Pitch 2 traverse; in lean or freeze-thaw years it can be dangerously thin or become bare rock/verglas, so check recent conditions closely rather than treating any given month as reliable.
routes.approach: Start at the Alpental Ski Area parking lot (~3,100 ft; I-90 Exit 52, north on Alpental Rd). Follow the Snow Lake Trail north into the valley on climber's-left of the outlet creek. In summer, stay on the maintained tread about 1.8-2 miles to the signed Source Lake Trail junction (~4,100 ft); in winter/spring the standard line leaves the summer trail earlier and climbs directly up the valley bottom/climbers'-path toward Source Lake — do not follow the exact summer boot path once there's meaningful snow cover, since it crosses avalanche terrain. From the Source Lake junction, leave the maintained trail and pick up the cairned climbers' path/talus traverse that runs above and around the east side of Source Lake, staying below the cliff band, aiming toward The Tooth's northeast aspect. Continue into the basin beneath the NE Face and ascend the broad snow finger/gully ("snow cone") that leads directly to the base of the Northeast Slabs route on the NE Face — cache skis in the hollow below and left of the route start before racking up. Figure roughly 2-2.5 miles and 1,500-2,000 ft of gain from the trailhead to the base of the climb; parties commonly do trailhead-to-summit-and-back in 4-6 hours in good firm-snow conditions. Hazards: this valley (Source Lake basin and the slopes below The Tooth) carries a well-documented history of avalanche accidents, rated "Challenging" avalanche terrain — assess stability seriously, especially in the transitional April-June snowpack the route is often climbed in, and do not treat the summer path as safe once snow is present. There are one or two creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet that can require removing skis or careful rock-hopping in high early-season flow. Above the talus the route-finding is cairned/boot-track only (no maintained tread), which can be tricky in whiteout or fresh snow.
routes.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb a short distance to the tree anchor in the small notch just below the true summit. From there, rappel the South Face line to the notch (Pineapple Pass) between The Tooth and its south sub-summit — four rappels of under 30 m on a single 60 m rope, or two long ones with two 60 m ropes; parties often note the second rappel can pull stiffly, so flake the rope and check your pull direction before committing. Some parties instead rappel off a chockstone lower on the gully, but this is described as less efficient than the tree-anchor double rappel and is not the standard line. From the notch you join the South Face (standard) descent: downclimb/walk the gully and talus down through Great Scott Bowl, then retrace the approach traverse back above Source Lake to the Snow Lake/Source Lake trail and the Alpental lot. In good winter/spring coverage this whole descent from the notch is frequently skied or glissaded — parties report as little as ~10 minutes from the notch back to the car on skis in prime conditions; on foot through talus, plan on more like 45-60 minutes. The same avalanche exposure noted on the approach applies to the descent, and expect possible traffic from parties climbing the South Face route if your lines overlap near Pineapple Pass.
routes.bail: The lower slab pitches can generally be down-climbed or rappelled from natural gear/ice screw anchors. Above the North Ridge notch, retreat becomes more involved; parties should be prepared to build rappel anchors from available rock/ice gear, or push on to the summit and descend via the South Face gully if that is more practical than reversing the route.

itinerary.cal: Climbed almost exclusively in winter/early spring when the slabs hold bonded snow/ice; a dry or lean-snow year leaves the route poorly protected and is best avoided.

days.note: Approach via the Source Lake trail (often skinned or skied in winter), then traverse south into the valley below The Tooth's east face to the base of the Northeast Slabs. Climb 5-6 pitches of low 5th-class rock and moderate, condition-dependent snow/ice up the obvious NE-facing slab to the North Ridge, then finish to the summit near the notch below the top. Descend the standard South Face rappel line back down to Pineapple Pass and hike out. This winter/spring mixed line is more serious than the South Face — protection on the slab pitches is sparse and run-out.

Carpools of 3+ can often park free as space allows.
access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Standard USFS wilderness group-size limit of 12 people (combined with stock) per party where the peak is inside Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

road.seasonalGate: No seasonal gate, but in winter the Alpental lot runs under the paid 'Park at the Summit' program on weekends and a handful of holidays only (roughly $25/vehicle), rather than accepting a Forest Pass.

climate.fall: Freeze-thaw cycles can rebuild ice, but conditions are less consistent than spring.
climate.spring: Often the prime season — slabs more likely to hold consolidated neve/ice for the route's namesake mixed climbing.
climate.summer: Slabs typically melt out to bare, often wet or loose rock; the route is rarely climbed once ice cover is gone, and most parties shift to the South Face instead.
climate.winter: Full winter mixed/ice conditions with significant avalanche hazard on the Source Lake approach if off the standard track.
climate.typical: Alpental is one of the snowiest ski areas in the Northwest (roughly 300-400+ in of snow in an average winter), so this route sits in serious avalanche terrain for much of its season.

bySeason.spring: Warming temperatures can either consolidate the snowpack into good neve or strip the route to bare rock/verglas.
bySeason.winter: Deep, often unstable snowpack; avalanche hazard on the approach can be significant — check NWAC before going.

emergency.notes: NWAC's Snoqualmie Pass Backcountry radio program (with Ski Patrol Rescue Team) monitors emergency traffic in this area during winter. Cell coverage in the basin is inconsistent.
emergency.rangerStation: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District (North Bend, WA)
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital (24/7 ER), 9801 Frontier Ave SE, Snoqualmie, WA — roughly 30-40 minutes' drive from Alpental via I-90.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: King County Sheriff's Office / King County Search & Rescue — call 911; non-emergency (206) 296-3311.

crowds.estimatePerSeason: unknown - low-traffic; rarely reported climbed relative to the summer South Face

routes.corrections: The supplied peak record had elevationFt as null. Wikipedia (5,606 ft / 1,708 m) and Mountain-Forecast.com (1,708 m / 5,610 ft) independently agree on the summit elevation, so 5,606 ft was used as highPointFt. Note Mountain Project's area page lists a lower, likely imprecise figure of 5,082 ft for the same peak — not used, since it's contradicted by two independent, closer-agreeing sources.

rappel_detail.pull: Check the pull direction before the last person leaves the anchor, and keep the strands out of the clefts beside the line.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel of the standard South Face descent that Northeast Slabs climbers join at the summit.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree in a notch at the summit's southeast edge
hazards: This is the pull that hangs up most often on the descent; at least one party has had to prusik back up the stuck strand to free it
Wide clefts in the rock flanking the line will swallow a thrown rope end - feed the rope down rather than tossing it
rappel_detail.station: From the summit, facing back down the climbing route, a short step down and to the left lands in the small notch on the southeast edge. The tree growing in that notch is the standard top anchor and normally already carries slings and rings. The rappel drops back onto the ledge where pitch 3 finishes.

rappel_detail.notes: Uses a single 60m rope; reported to come up just slightly short of the next anchor, requiring brief unroped scrambling.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree anchor at the pitch-3 ledge
hazards: A 60 m rope doubled (a 30 m rappel) finishes just short of the next tree, so the last few metres are an unroped down-scramble - expect it rather than discovering it at the rope ends. The scramble itself is short and surrounded by trees
rappel_detail.station: The anchor on the ledge at the top of pitch 3, right where the first rappel deposits you. The ground below is scrambly, but exposed enough that most parties rappel it rather than downclimb.

rappel_detail.pull: The tree sits back about two metres from the lip, so the rope saws across the flat top of the ledge and this pull can be very stiff. Pull from immediately at the slung rock horn atop pitch 1 - moving any further from the ledge before pulling is what makes it stick.
rappel_detail.notes: Long-used tree anchor; some parties worry about its long-term health.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree anchor at the pitch-2 ledge (a rock-anchor supplement has reportedly been added alongside the aging tree)
hazards: The tree is an ageing anchor carrying most of the traffic on the peak; use the rock backup beside it where it is in place
rappel_detail.station: The large, straight tree on the skier's-left side of the ledge where pitch 2 ends - the long-standing rappel tree on this descent. Since August 2024 a rock-based anchor has been added alongside it, because the tree is ageing under heavy traffic.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel back to the base of the South Face route near Pineapple Pass.
hazards: The anchor is a balanced block on a horn rather than fixed hardware; load it in line with the pull and do not shock-load or shift it
rappel_detail.station: Slung blocks at the top of pitch 1 - a balanced tabletop rock resting on a slung horn - which is also where you pull the previous rope from. The rappel returns you to the spot where you first roped up.

routes.rappel_count_note: Four rappels on a single 60 m rope, each under 30 m, reversing the four pitches of the South Face - this is the standard descent that Northeast Slabs parties join at the summit. Two 60 m ropes let you link them into fewer, longer raps. A separate two-rappel option exists in the east gully off Pineapple Pass on two bolted chain stations (60 m rope); its second station is not directly below the first, so you rappel out east and may have to scramble a few feet up a rib to reach it - that is a different line, not part of the four-rappel tree sequence above. Some winter parties instead take two long 60 m rappels from a tree below the summit straight down to the notch.

approach_variants.name: Alpental valley to the northeast basin (winter)
approach_variants.notes: From the Alpental upper lot (about 3,100 ft), go up the valley on the left side of the creek toward Source Lake, following the Source Lake line and whatever ski or boot track exists. In winter this means the valley bottom rather than the summer switchbacks, which cross the valley's avalanche chutes. Beyond Source Lake, climb the snow finger into the basin on the Tooth's northeast side, then continue up the snow slope beneath the face. Skis are normally cached at the bottom of that slope. Route-finding above the talus is cairn and boot-track only — there is no maintained tread — so fresh snow or a whiteout removes the only navigational aid you have.
approach_variants.season: Dec-Mar, and into spring on firm snow
hazards: Source Lake basin and the slopes below the Tooth have a documented avalanche accident history and are rated challenging avalanche terrain
the summer path is not a safe line once snow is present
thin, poorly protectable ice on the second pitch with long runouts
creek crossings near the Source Lake outlet at high flow
no maintained tread above the talus - navigation is by cairn and boot track only
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the foot of a distinct gully at the top of the snow slope on the northeast aspect. Pitch one climbs that gully; pitch two continues to the ridge crest above it; pitch three begins from a tree anchor on the ridge.

That tree is the confirmation. If the ground above your gully leads onto a bare rock rib with no trees on it, you have gone up the wrong feature — drop back to the snow and traverse. Likewise, if you are still on open snow with nothing gully-shaped above, you are short of the base; the slope continues.

The second pitch is the one to think about before committing: parties report thin ice, long runouts, and balancy mixed slab where screws and pickets are hard to place. Deciding at the base whether it is in condition is the real judgement call.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. It sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

routes.name: Upper Castle Toprope Wall

sectionBreakdown.note: This reads as a short roadside/approach toprope crag rather than a Rainier summit route — walk in, set up top-ropes, climb for a few hours, and return to the car the same day.
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Toprope session at Upper Castle Wall

routes.approach: Castle Rock stands beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth, with an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway around milepost 96.5. Take the climbers' trail starting on the west side of the lot. The trail climbs east across a broad ledge feature called Logger's Ledge, splitting the formation; the first routes are reachable in about 5-10 minutes of easy uphill walking. There's no named trail number and no water source at the crag — bring what you need.
routes.descent_text: As a toprope wall, there's no rappel involved in normal use — climbers are lowered off by their belayer after each route. If you need to walk to the top to rig anchors, the walk-off is a short scramble around the back/side of the formation back to the base trail; this is not described in detail anywhere, so treat it as a standard short crag walk-off and scout it before committing a party to the top.

road.name: US-2 through Tumwater Canyon, roadside pullout west of Leavenworth
road.status: Paved state highway with roadside parking — no forest road driving. The climbers' lot is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway, with no facilities and no water at the crag.
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth, head west on US-2 past the Icicle Creek Road junction and continue roughly two and a half miles into Tumwater Canyon. The pullout is on the right, and the climbers' trail starts at its west end and reaches the first routes in five to ten minutes of easy uphill walking.
road.seasonalGate: No seasonal gate — US-2 is maintained through the winter. The canyon is its own avalanche-control closure point, though, separate from Stevens Pass, and is closed on short notice after heavy snowfall; the pullout and the approach path also hold snow and ice well after the highway is clear.

approach_variants.name: West end of the pullout to Logger's Ledge
approach_variants.notes:
Castle Rock stands beside US-2 in Tumwater Canyon, about two to two and a half miles west of Leavenworth. There is an oversized dirt pullout on the north side of the highway at around milepost 96.5.

Take the trail from the uphill, western end of the pullout. It climbs and traverses east across the broad bench that splits the formation — Logger's Ledge — and reaches the first routes in five to ten minutes, the ledge itself in ten to fifteen.

There is no water at the crag and no named trail number.
approach_variants.season: Shoulder seasons, or early and late in the day
hazards: Full southwest sun; the formation faces predominantly southwest
Polished granite from very heavy traffic
No water at the crag
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The identifying feature for everything in this area is Logger's Ledge: a wide bench running across the middle of the formation, reached by an obvious trail from the west end of the parking area. Upper Castle routes are set up from that bench.

If you are at the base of the rock at road level you took the other trail — the one leaving the lower, eastern end of the same pullout, about fifty yards downhill — and you are at Lower Castle, a full wall too low.

Descent from anything topping out is a good climbers' trail off the back of the formation, returning to Logger's Ledge, and a trail from the ledge leads back to the parking area.
